87.t: New York as the center of everything; small-group record dates
87.s: Everything happened in New York, and he first recorded with small groups with Dizzy, Parker and Don Byas.
87.ch: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
87.q: But New York was a fun spot. This was a fun place. You wouldn't want to be anywhere else then because everything happened there. And all the bands that were on the road, they were just aching to get back to New York, not to make money, but where all the action was, you know? And it was really there.

87.t: Recording with Dizzy, Parker and Don Byas; Clyde Hart
87.s: Young recorded with Dizzy and Parker without working steadily with them, including "Can't Get Started," and with pianist-arranger Clyde Hart.
87.ch: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
87.q: But New York was interesting because on top of these things, though, you had a lot of opportunities to play with a lot of guys that you never did play regularly with, but you'd record with them.

455.s: Hawkins organizes a session with Dizzy, Clyde Hart and Howard McGhee; Budd arranges 'De Dakt' and Dizzy 'Woody 'n' You'.
455.q: back and -- from Europe and Coleman -- which, you know, was always a friend of mine. I had known Coleman since about 1926. And Coleman -- well, we lived around the corner from eachother. He lived in a place called the King Haven on 151st Street, and I lived at 152nd Street between Convent and…

455.t: Hawkins and Monk's tunes; first bop recordings
455.s: Hawkins was crazy about Monk, and the date he organizes yields among the first bop records.
455.q: But anyway these guys used to come around and hustle up different groups to make records, and at that time they had hustled Hawk up to make this record. Hawk wanted to be associated -- he was crazy about Thelonious Monk, and to my recollection Monk had the first modern tunes alive. I mean, if

368.t: Metronome All-Stars 1947 and his first bebop solo on Leap Here
368.s: He thinks his solo on Leap Here was his first recorded bebop solo, though he cannot recall the personnel.
368.q: No, no, not really because I did so many of those sessions and all the guys that were on those sessions kind of get mixed up after so many years. Like…

225.t: Records with Hawkins and Parker: Bean and the Boys and Crazeology
225.s: Baker asks about the Hawkins reissue and Crazeology; Johnson is vague on the chronology.
225.q: It could have been. That sounds familiar. The "Bean" part of it definitely sounds familiar. I’m just trying to think of the other part of the title. Feedin' the Bean might have been it.

228.t: The Dig recording session with Miles Davis
228.s: After the sit-in, McLean brings Dig to Miles's house, is hired with Sonny Rollins, and at the first session meets Mingus and is encouraged by Bird.
228.q: Right away, after I sat in with Miles on this Monday night, Tuesday afternoon I was at his house, because he gave me his phone number and address, said, “I want you to come by.” I went by. I showed him Dig. I had just written it. He picked it out and learned it. Then he asked me, did I know this,…

166.t: Monk, Klook Clarke and Minton's, and the first bop records
166.s: The Minton's house band, wire recordings, Hawkins's 'Woody'n You' and Dizzy's small-group sides.
166.ch: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York
166.q: Now, Klook Clarke was in this band at Minton's Playhouse. The band consisted of Monk on piano, Kermit Scott, tenor player, that's up in San Francisco now, Joe Guy on trumpet, Kenny Clarke on drums, and a bass player named Nick Penton. Now, Monk and Klook Clarke, they cooperated on these chords,…

92.t: Dizzy Gillespie recordings and being everyone's first-call guitarist
92.s: He made about fifty records with Jacquet and nearly all of Dizzy's, and Willard says he was everybody's first choice in New York.
92.ch: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
92.q: I can't think of the name of the tune, but it'll come to me. But any way, I must have made oh, 50 recordings with Jacket, Jacques "Emanon" you know, and Dizzy also. I did some very good -- this Imanon and just all of during that era. Yeah, sure all during that era. When John Lewis was playing…

428.t: Details of the Savoy bebop dates
428.s: Hall recalls the personnel of the Savoy dates, sponsor Herman Lubinsky, and how the guys were selling tunes cheaply.
428.q: Well, they were different than any recordings that I had been making. The versatility of the performance. I was in awe, as far as versatility was concerned. The rhythm section just had to be a (inaudible) one. A Ray Brown or Oscar Pettiford. (Unaudible)

413.t: Whiteman, Perez Prado, Dizzy, Armstrong and Parker
413.s: He re-recorded Rhapsody in Blue, played Prado's solo, and recorded with Dizzy, Armstrong and Parker.
